definition: Condone means to pardon or deliberately overlook wrongdoing.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word condone. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know condone should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Season after season the club fined no one for driving carts across the newly seeded greens, until members took the silence itself to condone the damage.
You can overlook a fault without ever knowing it was there; overlook stops short of condone, which sees the wrong clearly and lets it stand.
Applaud goes further than condone: to condone cheating is to let it pass in silence, while to applaud it is to celebrate the wrong out loud.

To tolerate is to put up with something you dislike — openly, and often while saying so. Condone is quieter and closer to guilt: whoever condones a wrong sees it clearly, says nothing, and lets the silence stand as permission. You can tolerate noise blamelessly; condoning cheating stains you.

To excuse is to accept a reason for a fault and let it go — the fault is admitted, weighed, and forgiven on its merits. Condone skips the weighing: it lets a wrong pass without consequence, and it belongs to onlookers and authorities whose silence gives the wrong its permission.
to ban the behavior before it happens

When a family donates books to the library, the gift is given outright — nothing owed, nothing asked back.
Condone means to pardon or deliberately overlook wrongdoing.

The academy's honor board found that a housemaster had known of the forged sick-notes for two full terms; by never reporting them he had condoned the forgery, the board ruled, and he was quietly retired.
Condone is subtler than 'approve': you may privately disapprove and still condone something by letting it pass without consequence.
Its object is almost always wrongdoing — you condone cheating or cruelty, never a kindness.
Condone sits in the middle of a tidy trio in this unit: abet helps a wrong along, condone lets it pass, and condemn — its near-twin in sound and its opposite in sense — calls it out.
Use condone for authorities and onlookers whose silence gives permission.

Every handbook of Harlow School forbade food in the dormitories, and every boy at Harlow knew the rule was dead.
For forty years the masters had walked slower on the last night of term, giving the famous midnight feast time to be tidied away.
Nothing was ever written down, and no master ever said the feast was allowed.
Yet by pausing on the stairs and asking no questions, the staff plainly condoned it, and the boys understood the silence exactly as it was meant.
When a new headmaster finally punished a feast in 1931, the outrage came not from the boys but from the old masters, who felt a forty-year bargain had been broken.
